newsitem.title: UGANDA: Ugandan economic growth on decline, ministers say.
newsitem.headline: Ugandan economic growth on decline, ministers say.

text.p: Uganda's booming economic growth is expected to slow this year with ministers and analysts blaming a variety of factors including smuggling, war and a poor work ethic.

Planning and Economic Development Minister Richard Kaijuka on Friday forecast gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1996/97 at 6.3 percent, lower than a target of 7.0 percent or the 8.5 percent growth attained in the previous year.
The Ugandan economy, rebounding from years of misrule, had previously registered 10 per cent growth for several years.
"According to what is on the ground, the economy has not performed very well. In fact, it was a downward trend," Minister of State for Economic Monitoring Syda Bumba said this week.
Bumba blamed the poor economic performance on inconsistences in implementing value added tax (VAT), a rise in smuggling due to prohibitive taxes and the absence of a strong work ethic.
She said people were putting in less hours at work.
Financial analysts also pointed to civil wars in northern and southeastern Uganda which they said ate into the budget.
"The population is expanding without our ability to expand production," Bumba told a Ugandan parliament committee but did not give the exact annual population growth.

Kaijuka said recent drought forced a slowdown in the growth rate with growth in food production dropping to 0.7 percent in 1996/97 from 4.4 percent in 1995/96. But he saw that decline as compensated for by faster growth in production of cash crops.
Kaijuka said there was a scarcity of money in rural areas because of lack of production of any tradeable goods.

He said manufacturing production in January was 30.7 percent higher than in January 1996 while the average sector growth for the first seven months of 1996/97 compared with the same period in the 1995/96 was 22.9 percent.
He said the projections for export earnings remained at the 1995/96 level of $590 million. He saw non-coffee exports as rising to $257 million in 1996/97 from $196 million in the previous year.
He said coffee exports would rise from four million 60-kg bags in 1995/96 to an estimated 4.4 million bags in 1996/97.
Kaijuka said data from Uganda Revenue Authority in the nine months to September 1996 showed a decline of 10 percent in the level of imports compared with the same period in 1995.

He said the financing of imports recorded by the central Bank of Uganda indicated that the volume of imports had remained at the same level as last year. He said a discrepancy between customs and bank data was explained by a rise in smuggling which he called "a national problem that must be addressed".
Kaijuka said as a percentage of GDP, recurrent revenue would rise from 11.4 percent in 1995/96 to 12.3 percent in 1996/97. He did not give a percentage or figures for recurrent expenditure.

Kaijuka said a reason for tax collections below estimates was a loss of efficiency in tax administration, as seen in a drop of income tax as a percentage of total revenue from 13.4 percent in 1995/96 to 12.3 percent in 1996/97.
